summary: Separate how long one item takes from how often items finish, and tie both to the slowest stage.
objective: Build a pipelined datapath where I can insert registers between stages and watch latency and throughput move in opposite directions.
intent_signals: Show why adding pipeline stages raises throughput but not latency.
Explain how the slowest stage sets the clock period.
example_prompts: Build a pipelined circuit where I can add pipeline registers and see latency and throughput update.
Show tokens flowing through a K-stage pipeline with a per-stage delay readout.
negative_signals: Not a processor microarchitecture recipe: hazards, forwarding and stalls are out of scope.
Not a performance measurement of any real device.
not_for: Not a processor microarchitecture recipe: hazards, forwarding and stalls are out of scope.

entities.name: Stage blocks
entities.guidance: Model each combinational stage as a block with its own delay value and an output register position that can be present or absent.

entities.name: Token flow
entities.guidance: Send identified tokens through the pipeline so the same item can be followed end to end while others enter behind it.

entities.name: Performance readout
entities.guidance: Display clock period, latency and throughput together, each derived from the current stage delays.

state_contract.model: A chain of combinational stages with finite positive delays and a register configuration. The clock period is the maximum stage delay over the current grouping, where removing a register merges contiguous blocks and sums their delays. Latency is reported both in clock periods (the stage count) and in model time units; throughput is reported both as one item per clock and as one over the period in items per model-time unit. The reciprocal is evaluated only for a finite positive period.
state_contract.authority: Stage delays and register placement are authoritative; the three performance numbers are always recomputed and never authored independently.
actions: Insert or remove a pipeline register between stages.
Change a stage delay and observe the clock period.
Follow one token through the pipeline.

invariants: Every path from input to output crosses the same number of registers; an unbalanced insertion is rejected.

The clock period equals the largest stage delay after the current grouping, so reducing one of several tied slowest stages leaves it unchanged; the period is compared against the recomputed maximum rather than against the edited stage.

Adding a register increases the latency measured in clock periods while throughput stays one item per clock; measured in model time the two need not move oppositely, since a perfectly balanced split can leave time latency unchanged and splitting a non-critical stage can leave throughput unchanged.
motion_guidance: Advance tokens one stage per clock tick with a visible tick marker; smooth continuous sliding hides the discrete nature of the pipeline.
Keep token identity visible across stages so latency can be observed for a specific item.
known_limits: Idealised pipeline with no hazards, no bubbles and zero register overhead beyond the declared delays.
Throughput here is per clock, not a wall-clock measurement.
Authored guidance only: no scene runtime, rendering or numerical calibration has been run for this recipe.

claims.statement: Latency is the time to process a particular input, and throughput is the rate at which the system produces outputs.
claims.scope: Definitions as taught for synchronous systems.

claims.statement: A K-stage pipeline has exactly K registers on every path from input to output, its latency is K times the clock period, its throughput is the clock frequency, and the clock period is set by the propagation delay of the slowest stage.
claims.scope: Well-formed synchronous pipeline as taught, with register overhead folded into the stated stage delays; the clock period follows the slowest stage, which need not be unique.

source_refs.locator: 7.1 slides, K-stage pipeline latency, throughput and clock period

object_craft.structure: Blocks arranged along a visible datapath rail with slots between them where registers can be dropped in.
object_craft.material: Uniform stage material so the slowest stage can be marked by a single reserved accent rather than by size.
object_craft.articulation: Registers appear and disappear in slots; stages themselves do not move.

object_craft.structure: Small labelled carriers that occupy exactly one stage at a time, with a queue indicator at the input.
object_craft.material: Per-token identity colour from a small repeating palette plus a printed index, so identity survives palette reuse.
object_craft.articulation: Tokens step one stage per tick and are removed at the output.

physical_contract.scope: Discrete tick-based token movement; no physical transport or contact.
checks: All input-to-output paths report the same register count.
Reducing the unique slowest stage delay reduces the clock period and raises throughput in items per model-time unit; with tied slowest stages the period is unchanged until every tie is reduced.
